papers.title_in_file: Efficient QAOA Architecture for Solving Multi-Constrained Optimization Problems
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results and conclusion read in full; later appendices skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A QAOA architecture combining XY-mixers for one-hot constraints with oracle-based indicator functions for inequality constraints, benchmarked in state vector simulation on multi-knapsack and prosumer problems.

assertions.value: The authors report that the combined constraint architecture gives better solution quality and a higher probability of sampling the optimal solution than the established QUBO formulation, and that the time-to-solution is more than an order of magnitude faster than the baseline methods.
quotes: We benchmark the combined method against the established QUBO formulation, yielding a better solution quality and probability of sampling the optimal solution.
Despite more complex circuits, the time-to-solution is more than an order of magnitude faster compared to the baseline methods and exhibits more favorable scaling properties.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation benchmark on two problem families; not a proof.
assertions.reader_inference: Results are simulated state vector benchmarks on multi-knapsack and prosumer instances only.

assertions.value: The authors state that one-hot constraints are enforced through XY-mixers that restrict the search space to the feasible subspace, and that inequality constraints are implemented through oracle-based Indicator Functions.
quotes: One-hot constraints are enforced through XY -mixers that restrict the search space to the feasible sub-space naturally.
Inequality constraints are implemented through oracle-based Indicator Functions (IF).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its method, Abstract p.1.

assertions.value: The authors report that their simulation enhancements allowed simulating instances of up to 88 binary variables and 14 inequality constraints.
quotes: we employ several enhancements to accelerate and enable simulation of problem instances that would be otherwise impossible to simulate, e.g., up to 88 binary variables and 14 inequality constraints.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of the scale of its own simulations, Section VI.
assertions.reader_inference: The results come from classical simulation at this scale, not from quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that the scaling of IF+XY is still remarkably close to random sampling from all one-hot constrained states, and that their evaluation was limited to p = 12.
assertions.anchor: Section V discussion and Section VI conclusion
quotes: However, the scaling of IF+XY is still remarkably close to the random sampling from all one-hot constrained states.
One reason is that we limit evaluation to p = 12; deeper layers could likely lead to better TTS.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit themselves, Sections V and VI.
assertions.reader_inference: The time-to-solution advantage may not carry to large instances if scaling stays near random sampling.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Circuits for High-Dimensional Absolutely Maximally Entangled States
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results and conclusion read in full; later appendices skimmed
papers.what_it_is: Explicit qudit circuits for non-stabilizer AME states of four subsystems with four, six and eight levels, with noise and teleportation analysis.

assertions.value: The authors present explicit quantum circuits that generate exemplary non-stabilizer AME states of four subsystems with four, six and eight levels each.
quotes: we present explicit quantum circuits to generate exemplary non-stabilizer AME states of four subsystems with four, six, and eight levels each and analyze their capabilities to perform quantum information tasks.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own contribution and scope, Abstract.

assertions.value: The authors state that AME states are characterized by maximal entanglement across all possible bipartitions of the system, so that every subset of particles is maximally entangled with its complementary subset.
quotes: AME states are characterized by maximal entanglement across all possible bipartitions of the system, ensuring that every subset of particles is maximally entangled with its complementary subset.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of AME states as used in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors report that, under depolarizing noise, the AME(4, 6) and AME(4, 4) states remain useful for teleportation up to noise levels of around 35%.
quotes: our findings concerning AME(4, 6) and AME(4, 4) states show that, up to noise levels of around 35%, both states even in the presence of noise are useful for teleportation
assertions.certainty_reason: A model-based noise analysis in one paper (depolarizing noise), not hardware data.
assertions.reader_inference: The figure holds only under the depolarizing noise model the authors assume.

assertions.value: The authors state that AME states have yet to be achieved experimentally and that there is no known physical process generating them or a known Hamiltonian whose ground state is an AME state.
quotes: have yet to be achieved experimentally
While AME states can be mathematically constructed and studied so far, there is no known physical process generating such states, or a known Hamiltonian whose ground state is an AME state.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of the limit of current knowledge, Section V.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results and conclusion read in full; later appendices skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A quantum LSTM used as the core of a deep recurrent Q-learning agent, tested in simulation on Cart-Pole.

assertions.value: The authors report numerical simulations in which the QLSTM-DRQN solves Cart-Pole with more stable and higher average scores than a classical DRQN with similar architecture and number of model parameters.
quotes: We demonstrate the results via numerical simulations that the QLSTM-DRQN can solve standard benchmark such as Cart-Pole with more stable and higher average scores than classical DRQN with similar architecture and number of model parameters.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulated study on one benchmark.
assertions.reader_inference: Single toy benchmark, simulation only, no noise; the paper gives no statistical test in the text read.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QLSTM uses 8-qubit VQCs with input and hidden dimension 4, that QLSTM with 1 or 2 VQC layers is considered, and that the test environment is Cart-Pole.
quotes: The QLSTM used in this paper includes 8-qubit VQCs. The input and hidden dimension of the QLSTM are both 4.
We consider QLSTM with 1 or 2 VQC layers
The testing environment we choose in this work is Cart-Pole
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup, Sections 6.1 and 6.3.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the partially observable Cart-Pole the classical LSTM with 16 hidden neurons collapses after 800 episodes of training while the QLSTM agents remain stable.
quotes: For example, the classical LSTM with 16 hidden neurons collapses after 800 episodes of training while the QLSTM agents remain stable.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulated study.
assertions.reader_inference: Based on a single reported training curve (Figure 5).

papers.title_in_file: Crossing The Gap Using Variational Quantum Eigensolver: A Comparative Study
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results and conclusion read in full; later appendices skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A comparison of VQD and SSVQE for low-lying excited states of LiH, of three optimizers, and a proposed folded-spectrum extension tested on H4.

assertions.value: The authors report that VQD exhibits a slight advantage in accuracy while SSVQE stands out for efficiency, finding all low-lying excited states of LiH through a single parameter optimization procedure; the conclusion states the two methods perform almost the same in accuracy.
quotes: Our investigation reveals that while VQD exhibits a slight advantage in accuracy, SSVQE stands out for its efficiency, allowing the determination of all low-lying excited states through a single parameter optimization procedure.
In terms of accuracy, the performance of VQD and SSVQE are almost the same.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical comparison on one molecule.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract and the conclusion describe the accuracy gap differently (slight advantage against almost the same).

assertions.value: The authors report that, among Gradient Descent, Quantum Natural Gradient and Adam, the Adam optimizer required the fewest iterations to obtain the first excited state of LiH.
quotes: We further evaluate the effectiveness of optimizers, including Gradient Descent (GD), Quantum Natural Gradient (QNG), and Adam optimizer, in obtaining LiH's first excited state, with the Adam optimizer demonstrating superior efficiency in requiring the fewest iterations.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on one molecule and state.

assertions.value: The authors report that Folded Spectrum SSVQE can find all three highly excited states of H4 near −1.0 Ha with only one optimizing procedure but converges slowly, while Folded Spectrum VQD uses individual procedures that converge faster.
quotes: Folded Spectrum SSVQE (FS-SSVQE) can find all three highly excited states near −1.0 Ha with only one optimizing procedure, but the procedure converges slowly.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on one molecule.

assertions.value: The authors state that the study compares VQD and SSVQE on the low-lying excited states of LiH, tests the new approaches on the excited states of H4, and leaves the effectiveness on larger molecules for future research.
quotes: In this study, we compare the performance of Variational Quantum Deflation (VQD) and SubspaceSearch Variational Quantum Eigensolver (SSVQE) methods in determining the low-lying excited states of LiH.
It is crucial to investigate the effectiveness of VQD and SSVQE methodologies when applied to larger chemical molecules
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of scope and what it leaves open.

papers.title_in_file: Scalable Community Detection Using Quantum Hamiltonian Descent and QUBO Formulation
papers.version_note: The file name says Quantum Hamiltonian Descent for Graph Partition (arXiv 2411.14696) but the file text is v3, titled Scalable Community Detection Using Quantum Hamiltonian Descent and QUBO Formulation, matching the record id.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results and conclusion read in full; later appendices skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A quantum-inspired QHD solver, run on GPUs, for modularity-based community detection as a QUBO, compared with GUROBI on CPUs.

assertions.value: The authors report that their method achieves up to 5.49% better modularity scores while requiring less computational time compared to classical optimization approaches.
quotes: Benchmarking shows our method achieves up to 5.49% better modularity scores while requiring less computational time compared to classical optimization approaches.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; the authors' own benchmark.
assertions.reader_inference: The method is quantum-inspired and runs on classical GPUs, so it does not bear on quantum hardware advantage.

assertions.value: The authors report that in 199 instances where GUROBI found proven optimal solutions QHD matched them in 75.4% of cases, and that in 739 instances where GUROBI hit its time limit QHD found better solutions in 71.4% of cases and matching solutions in another 17.2%.
quotes: In the 199 cases where GUROBI found proven optimal solutions (typically smaller problems with mean size of 54 variables), QHD matched these optimal solutions in 75.4% of cases.

More importantly, in the larger set of 739 instances where GUROBI hit its time limit (predominantly larger problems with mean size of 614 variables), QHD demonstrated superior performance by finding better solutions in 71.4% of cases and matching GUROBI's solutions in another 17.2%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the algorithm is quantum-inspired and uses Quantum Hamiltonian Descent, that QHD ran on four NVIDIA A5000 GPUs while GUROBI ran on CPUs, and that GUROBI was given the same time limit as QHD's execution time.
quotes: We present a quantum-inspired algorithm that utilizes Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD) for efficient community detection.
Implementation of QHD on QUBO is running with four NVIDIA A5000 GPUs and the comparison with GUROBI is conducted with CPUs as mentioned.
first measuring QHD's execution time, then allocating GUROBI the same as its time limit.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own method and test setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison pairs GPUs against CPUs, so it does not isolate algorithmic difference.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the sparsest large network, LastFM with density 0.0010, GUROBI outperforms QHD by 3.79%.
quotes: Notably, in the sparsest network, LastFM (density 0.0010), GUROBI outperforms QHD by 3.79%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on one network.

papers.title_in_file: Evidence for effectively constant shot complexity in the quantum approximate optimization algorithm without per-instance optimization
papers.version_note: The file name carries the v1 title (Improving QAOA to find approximate QUBO solutions in O(1) shots), but the file text is v3 titled Evidence for effectively constant shot complexity ..., matching the record id.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results and conclusion read in full; later appendices skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A fixed-point QAOA with classically trained parameters transferred to larger instances, studied by noiseless simulation up to 30 qubits on random QUBO ensembles.

assertions.value: The authors report from noiseless simulations up to 30 qubits on random QUBO ensembles that the median number of shots needed to reach approximation ratio 0.95 decreases towards a nearly constant value as problem size increases.
quotes: Noiseless numerical simulations (for system sizes up to 30 qubits) across a variety of random QUBO ensembles
decreases towards a nearly constant value as the problem size increases
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from simulation on random ensembles; the authors state it is not a proof.
assertions.reader_inference: Simulation only, noiseless, with depth scaled linearly with problem size.

assertions.value: The authors report that removing any single component of the scheme restores rapid growth of the required number of shots, which they describe as the synergistic nature of the three modifications.
quotes: Moreover, removing any single component of the scheme restores rapid growth of the required number of shots, highlighting the synergistic nature of the three modifications.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical ablation in one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the approach is heuristic, that they do not claim a rigorous constant-complexity result, that the analysis is restricted to simulations up to n = 30 qubits, and that the simulations contain no noise.
quotes: First, the proposed approach remains heuristic in nature.
Second, the present analysis is restricted to numerical simulations with system sizes up to n = 30 qubits.
Another important limitation is the absence of noise in the current simulations of the sampling stage.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors list these limits themselves, Section V.

assertions.value: The authors state that they study a modified fixed-point QAOA in which parameters are trained classically on small instances and then transferred to larger problems.
quotes: We study a modified fixed-point version of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (fpQAOA), where parameters are trained classically on small instances and then transferred to larger problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own method.

papers.title_in_file: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm Can Require Exponential Time to Optimize Linear Functions
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results and conclusion read in full; later appendices skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A mathematical argument that QAOA with a bounded number of layers needs exponential time on certain linear Ising functions, with a conjecture for general p.

assertions.value: The paper proves (Theorem 1), for a number of layers p that is a constant independent of the problem size n, that if no choice of angle vectors of size p makes the optimal solution of a linear Ising model certain, then we can build a family of linear Ising models for which the QAOA runtime grows exponentially with the problem size n.
quotes: Let the number of layers in the ansatz of QAOA, p, be a constant independent of the problem size n
then we can build a family of linear Ising models for which the QAOA runtime grows exponentially with the problem size n.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1, p.6 (a conditional statement with a proof).
assertions.reader_inference: The theorem is conditional on a coefficient vector whose optimal-state probability stays below one for every angle choice; the paper proves this only for p = 1 and p = 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that they prove the condition for p = 1 and p = 2 and do not have a proof for p > 2.
quotes: We will prove here that this is the case for p = 1 and p = 2. We do not have, at the moment, a proof for p > 2, only the results shown in Subsection 3.1.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their own proof, Section 3 p.7.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract's claim about exponential time at all p below n rests on a conjecture beyond p = 2.

assertions.value: The authors conjecture that QAOA needs exponential time to find the global optimum of linear functions for any constant value of p.
quotes: We conjecture that QAOA needs exponential time to find the global optimum of linear functions for any constant value of p
assertions.certainty_reason: A conjecture supported by numerical maximization for small p, not proved.

assertions.value: The authors state that they assume perfect quantum computers with no noise and an oracle that provides the optimal angle parameters, so that the runtime they obtain is a lower bound of the real runtime of QAOA for any classical optimization algorithm.
quotes: We should clarify here that we assume throughout the paper that we can get perfect quantum computers with no noise, and this is the context in which our results hold.
In practice, this means that the runtime we will obtain is a lower bound of the real runtime of QAOA for any classical optimization algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state their own assumptions and scope.

papers.title_in_file: Energy Landscapes for the Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results and conclusion read in full; later appendices skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A study of QAOA cost landscapes for Max-Cut on small graphs using basin-hopping and discrete path sampling, with new performance metrics.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QAOA landscapes they studied generally have a single funnel organisation, which makes it relatively straightforward to locate low-lying minima with good Max-Cut solution probabilities.
quotes: We find that the corresponding landscapes generally have a single funnel organisation, which makes it relatively straightforward to locate low-lying minima with good Max-Cut solution probabilities.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on a small set of graphs.
assertions.reader_inference: The graphs studied are small (up to eight vertices), so the result may not carry to large instances.

assertions.value: The authors report that in some cases below the adiabatic limit the second lowest local minimum may yield a higher solution probability than the global minimum.
quotes: In some cases below the adiabatic limit the second lowest local minimum may even yield a higher solution probability than the global minimum.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical observation on specific graphs.

assertions.value: The authors state that they performed 10,000 basin-hopping steps per run for the unweighted graphs K3 − K8 and 6a−8e and the weighted graphs G2−G5, using the GMIN program for varying L.
quotes: For each basin-hopping optimisation run, we performed 10,000 basin-hopping steps for the unweighted graphs K3 − K8, 6a−8e, and for the weighted graphs G2−G5, using the GMIN program for varying L.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own computational setup, Appendix A.

assertions.value: The authors recommend choosing L = 3 layers to solve Max-Cut for the weighted graphs G2 − G5.
quotes: Hence, as for K5 − K8, we recommend choosing L = 3 in solving the Max-Cut problem for G2 − G5.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author recommendation drawn from their metric on four small graphs.
